## Recap

- CNNs are the backbone of most computer vision models
- Many different model architectures
- Different computer vision "tasks" - from image classification to depth estimation

## How do we run these models?

- A better question to ask is "Where do we run these models?"

## Running models on the edge

- Most realtime computer vision tasks need to run on the "edge"
  - Dedicated hardware, very close to the camera source
  - e.g., Raspberry Pi with camera or your iPhone
  - Model inference on the edge; only results (detections, metadata) sent back to the server

## Running models on the edge

- Why not stream the video feed back to a central server?
  - **Bandwidth** - very high for video data streams
  - **Latency** - many applications need to react quickly

## Running models on the edge

- This introduces two requirements:
  - Models need to be interoperable to run on different hardware platforms
  - Models need to be optimized to run on lower-powered devices (e.g., quantization)

## Running models on the edge

- Four popular formats:
  - TensorRT - NVIDIA's inference engine for NVIDIA GPUs (e.g., Jetson)
  - Core ML - Apple's framework for iOS, macOS, and other Apple devices
  - LiteRT (formerly TFLite) - Google's lightweight runtime for mobile and embedded
  - ONNX - Open, interoperable format from Microsoft and Meta

## ONNX

- Open Neural Network Exchange
  - Open standard created by Microsoft and Facebook (2017)
  - Now governed by the Linux Foundation (LF AI & Data)
- Model saved as a computation graph (`.onnx` file)
  - Built from a standard set of operators, so any compatible runtime can run it
- Export from most frameworks (PyTorch, TensorFlow, scikit-learn)

## ONNX

- ONNX Runtime runs models almost anywhere
  - Windows, Linux, macOS, iOS, Android, and the browser
  - Uses the hardware's accelerators (e.g., CUDA, TensorRT, Core ML)
- Also supports quantization (e.g., FP32 to INT8)

## Acquiring these models

- Convert from the original model format (e.g., PyTorch) to desired format

  ```python
  import torch, torchvision

  model = torchvision.models.resnet18(weights="DEFAULT").eval()
  dummy_input = torch.randn(1, 3, 224, 224)  # batch, channels, height, width
  torch.onnx.export(model, dummy_input, "resnet18.onnx")
  ```

## Acquiring these models 

- Download a model that has already been converted
  - [Hugging Face models filtered by ONNX](https://huggingface.co/models?library=onnx){.external target="blank"}

## ONNX in the Browser

- With similar constraints to edge hardware, ONNX models can also run in the browser!
- How this works:
  - Download ONNX model from Hugging Face
  - Load the model into OpenCV's dnn module
  - Create a detect function to run the model and map to classes
  - Bind the detect function to the Webcam (if running on a live stream)

# Challenges with computer vision

## Challenges with computer vision

- While many CV models are amazing, computer vision in real world environments can be challenging
  - Power/compute
  - Lens design and lighting
  - Object tracking and persistence

## Power/compute

- Models will always run slower (or consume more power) than you would like
  - Example: Camera setup on 12V vehicle battery
- Mitigation:
  - Optimizing the model (input layer size, output classes) for the hardware stack
  - Testing on actual hardware as soon as possible

## Lens design and lighting

- Edge camera lens is often different to the lens used to train the model
  - Example: Wider FOV for device lens vs. training lens
- Different lighting conditions can negatively impact detection rates
  - Example: Detecting road objects in daytime/nighttime/rainy conditions

## Lens design and lighting 

- Mitigation:
  - Train your models using the same camera as you'll use on the edge (record and label your own training videos)
  - Ensure your training data includes a variety of different lighting conditions

## Object tracking and persistence

- Many models can be used with a separate tracker (such as ByteTrack), but persistence when occluded can be challenging
  - Example: Stop signs occluded by trees or road objects with windshield wiper
- Mitigation:
  - Start with ByteTrack and training data. Implement relative localization if not enough.
  - Use projected paths and/or boundaries to determine unique objects

## Summary

- Realtime CV models usually run on the edge, close to the camera
  - Saves bandwidth and reduces latency
- Edge models need to be interoperable and optimized
  - Popular formats: TensorRT, Core ML, LiteRT, and ONNX
  - ONNX is an open standard that runs almost anywhere, including the browser

## Summary 

- Convert models from PyTorch, or download pre-converted models from Hugging Face
- Real world challenges: power/compute, lens and lighting, and object tracking
  - Test early on actual hardware, with the actual camera, in real conditions
